chunk_text: This packet orients new professional stagehands in their first 0-24 months. It is not a certification, safety manual, legal compliance guide, or authorization to perform restricted tasks.

The common production lifecycle is load-in, show call, and load-out. Load-in involves unloading, staging, assembly, cabling, testing, and preparation. Show call emphasizes quiet standby, cue discipline, and assigned operation. Load-out is fast and fatigue-heavy, so workers must slow down around energized systems, flown systems, heavy equipment, and truck zones.

Day-one stagehand competence means safe, coachable, and useful: PPE readiness, clear communication, safe material handling, basic cable care, jobsite awareness, and respect for chain of command. The first 24 months should progress from orientation to useful generalist to controlled department specialization.

Non-negotiable safety standards include situational awareness, assigned PPE, hazard recognition, avoiding suspended-load exposure, and refusing to self-authorize restricted tasks. Forklifts, aerial lifts, rigging, motor control, fall arrest systems, power distribution, pyrotechnics, lasers, and rope access commonly require formal training, certification, or site-specific authorization.

Unspoken rules include being useful before impressive, not touching another department's gear without direction, staying visible to the lead, not faking knowledge, keeping radio traffic short, and treating corrections as normal jobsite learning.

Underestimated beginner risks include fatigue, hearing exposure, weather, mental load, informal pressure, truck/dock zones, and public-interface work zones. Load-out is especially risky because speed, darkness, fatigue, and heavy gear often combine.

In the first 90 days, learn department names, stage directions, PPE expectations, radio etiquette, cable coiling, and chain of command. Master on-time check-in, safe case pushing, basic cable safety, clean work zones, and asking before touching restricted systems.

House stagehands know venue systems, local rules, house gear, and building-specific constraints. Touring stagehands know the show package, truck pack, repeatable workflow, and touring system. Local crew usually adapts to the show; road crew usually protects consistency across changing venues.

Priority research areas include OSHA worker rights, PPE, fall protection, hazard communication, walking-working surfaces, electrical safety, powered industrial trucks, aerial lift requirements, ESTA/ANSI E1 standards, ETCP certification pathways, IATSE local structure, department technical basics, hearing conservation, heat stress, fatigue, and mental health.

For unsafe or high-pressure situations: pause, identify the hazard, protect yourself and others if safe, report to the appropriate lead or safety contact, clarify the authorized method, remember who gave the instruction, and resume only when the hazard control is clear.
